title: The Video Game That Helps Teens Feel Better
summary: Can a video game help teenagers feel better? A new study says yes, if the game supports mental well-being. The game is called PlaySmart. In one scene, friend Taylor has drifted away, and the player feels it might be their fault. PlaySmart was made by the play2PREVENT Lab to give teens tools for mental-health struggles or opioid drug misuse. It was tested like scientists test medicines, in a trial with volunteers. The findings were shared on August 17 in JAMA Network Open. The team brought the games to 15 Connecticut high schools. Students were randomly assigned to play PlaySmart or a different game, such as The Sims. Everyone played once or twice a week for six weeks. Teens who played PlaySmart had fewer depression symptoms a year later. They also knew more about opioid drugs and were more open to getting help from a therapist or counsellor. Researchers think knowing help is available may be part of why the game helped. Linda Charmaraman of Wellesley College, who did not help build the game, called the year-long effect very promising.
why_it_matters: It shows a game you play could also teach you ways to feel better and where to ask for help when you are struggling.

background_read: Teenagers can face worries and low feelings, and they may need tools to help them cope and to know where to get help.
PlaySmart is a video game made to give teens tools for mental-health struggles and to teach them about drug misuse.
In a trial, some teens played PlaySmart and others played a different game, so scientists could compare how the groups felt later.
Article_Structure: WHO: Teenagers at 15 Connecticut high schools, researchers from the play2PREVENT Lab, and Linda Charmaraman of Wellesley College.
WHAT: They tested PlaySmart, a video game made to give teens tools for mental-health struggles and opioid drug misuse, against a different game.
WHY: To see if a game that supports mental well-being could help teens feel better and know more about getting help.
